_link.title: I can describe and identify from diagrams the four stages of mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase

toLevel2.question: What is the correct order of the four stages of mitosis?

options.text: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
options.explanation: The four stages follow the PMAT order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

options.text: Metaphase, anaphase, prophase, telophase
options.explanation: This order is incorrect. Prophase comes first, followed by metaphase, anaphase, then telophase.

options.text: Anaphase, telophase, prophase, metaphase
options.explanation: This order is incorrect. The correct sequence is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

options.text: Telophase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase
options.explanation: This order is incorrect. Telophase is the final stage, not the first.

options.text: Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nuclear membrane breaks down
options.explanation: In prophase, chromatin condenses into chromosomes, the nuclear membrane breaks down, and centrosomes move to opposite poles.

options.text: Chromosomes line up along the metaphase plate at the cell equator
options.explanation: Chromosome alignment at the equator occurs during metaphase, not prophase.

options.text: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell by spindle fibres
options.explanation: Chromatid separation occurs during anaphase, not prophase.

options.text: Nuclear membranes re-form around each group of chromosomes in the cell
options.explanation: Nuclear membrane reformation occurs during telophase, not prophase.

toLevel2.question: During which stage of mitosis do chromosomes line up along the metaphase plate?

options.text: Metaphase
options.explanation: During metaphase, double chromosomes align along the metaphase plate (equator) of the cell.

options.text: Prophase
options.explanation: During prophase, chromosomes condense but have not yet aligned at the equator.

options.text: Anaphase
options.explanation: During anaphase, chromosomes are being pulled apart, not lining up at the equator.

options.text: Telophase
options.explanation: During telophase, chromosomes are decondensing at the poles, not lining up at the equator.

toLevel2.question: What occurs during anaphase of mitosis?

options.text: Centromeres split and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
options.explanation: In anaphase, centromeres split and spindle fibres pull sister chromatids to opposite poles of the cell.

options.text: Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes inside the nucleus
options.explanation: Chromatin condensation occurs during prophase, not anaphase.

options.text: Chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell on the plate
options.explanation: Chromosome alignment occurs during metaphase, not anaphase.

options.text: Nuclear membranes re-form and chromosomes decondense to chromatin
options.explanation: Nuclear membrane reformation and decondensation occur during telophase, not anaphase.

options.text: Chromosomes decondense and nuclear membranes re-form around each group
options.explanation: In telophase, chromosomes decondense to chromatin and nuclear membranes re-form, producing two nuclei.

options.text: The nuclear membrane breaks down and centrosomes move to opposite poles
options.explanation: Nuclear membrane breakdown and centrosome movement occur during prophase, not telophase.

options.text: Centromeres split and sister chromatids separate to opposite poles
options.explanation: Centromere splitting and chromatid separation occur during anaphase, not telophase.

options.text: Double chromosomes align at the metaphase plate in the cell centre
options.explanation: Chromosome alignment at the equator occurs during metaphase, not telophase.

toLevel2.question: During prophase, the nuclear membrane breaks down and chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Prophase involves chromatin condensation, nuclear membrane breakdown, and centrosome migration to poles.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. Prophase is characterised by chromatin condensation and nuclear membrane breakdown.

toLevel2.question: During metaphase, sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles during anaphase, not metaphase. Metaphase involves chromosome alignment.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. Sister chromatids are pulled apart during anaphase. During metaphase, chromosomes line up at the equator.

toLevel2.question: During prophase, chromatin {{blank:1}} into visible chromosomes and the nuclear {{blank:2}} breaks down.

options.text: condenses
options.explanation: Chromatin condenses (coils tightly) to form visible, distinct chromosomes during prophase.

options.text: dissolves
options.explanation: Chromatin does not dissolve; it condenses into tightly coiled visible chromosomes.

options.text: replicates
options.explanation: DNA replication occurs during S phase, not prophase. Prophase involves condensation.

options.text: membrane
options.explanation: The nuclear membrane (envelope) breaks down during prophase, allowing spindle access to chromosomes.

options.text: ribosome
options.explanation: Ribosomes are not a membrane structure. The nuclear membrane breaks down during prophase.

options.text: cytoplasm
options.explanation: The cytoplasm is not a membrane. The nuclear membrane breaks down during prophase.

toLevel2.question: During anaphase, {{blank:1}} split and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite {{blank:2}}.

options.text: centromeres
options.explanation: Centromeres split during anaphase, releasing sister chromatids to be pulled to opposite poles.

options.text: ribosomes
options.explanation: Ribosomes are not involved in chromosome separation. Centromeres split during anaphase.

options.text: nucleoli
options.explanation: The nucleolus disappears during prophase. Centromeres split during anaphase.

options.text: poles
options.explanation: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell by spindle microtubules.

options.text: nuclei
options.explanation: Nuclei have not yet reformed; chromatids are pulled to opposite poles during anaphase.

options.text: plates
options.explanation: The metaphase plate is where chromosomes align. During anaphase, chromatids move to the poles.

toLevel2.question: During telophase, chromosomes {{blank:1}} to chromatin and nuclear membranes {{blank:2}} around each group.

options.text: decondense
options.explanation: Chromosomes decondense (uncoil) back into chromatin during telophase.

options.text: condense
options.explanation: Condensation occurs during prophase; telophase involves decondensation.

options.text: replicate
options.explanation: Replication occurs during S phase; telophase involves chromosomes decondensing.

options.text: re-form
options.explanation: Nuclear membranes re-form around each set of chromosomes, producing two distinct nuclei.

options.text: dissolve
options.explanation: Nuclear membranes dissolve during prophase; they re-form during telophase.

options.text: thicken
options.explanation: Nuclear membranes re-form during telophase, not simply thicken.

toLevel3.question: Why must the nuclear membrane break down during prophase?

options.text: So that spindle microtubules can access and attach to the chromosomes
options.explanation: The nuclear membrane must break down so spindle fibres from centrosomes can reach and attach to chromosome kinetochores.

options.text: So that DNA replication can occur inside the nucleus during mitosis
options.explanation: DNA replication occurs during S phase, not during mitosis. The breakdown allows spindle access.

options.text: So that the cell can absorb nutrients from the surrounding environment
options.explanation: Nutrient absorption is not the reason for nuclear membrane breakdown during prophase.

options.text: So that chromosomes can be exported out of the cell during division
options.explanation: Chromosomes remain inside the cell; the breakdown allows spindle fibres to attach to them.

toLevel3.question: Why is it important that chromosomes align at the metaphase plate before anaphase begins?

options.text: Alignment ensures each sister chromatid can be pulled equally to opposite poles
options.explanation: Proper alignment at the equator ensures even distribution of chromatids when they separate during anaphase.

options.text: Alignment is not important and chromosomes can separate from any position
options.explanation: Alignment is essential for equal distribution; without it, daughter cells may receive unequal chromosomes.

options.text: Alignment allows chromosomes to replicate one more time before separating
options.explanation: Chromosomes do not replicate at metaphase; they were already replicated in S phase.

options.text: Alignment causes the chromosomes to fuse together permanently at the equator
options.explanation: Chromosomes do not fuse; they align for orderly separation during anaphase.

toLevel3.question: How can you distinguish a cell in interphase from a cell in prophase when viewing a micrograph?

options.text: Interphase shows a clear nucleus with dark mass; prophase shows individual chromosomes without a nuclear membrane
options.explanation: In interphase, the nucleus is intact with diffuse chromatin. In prophase, condensed chromosomes are visible and the nuclear membrane is absent.

options.text: Interphase cells are always larger than prophase cells in every case
options.explanation: Size alone does not distinguish phases; the key difference is the nuclear membrane and chromosome visibility.

options.text: Prophase cells have two nuclei while interphase cells have one nucleus
options.explanation: Two nuclei form during telophase, not prophase. Prophase shows condensed chromosomes without a clear nuclear membrane.

options.text: There is no visible difference between interphase and prophase in micrographs
options.explanation: The key difference is the nuclear membrane and chromosome condensation state.

toLevel3.question: Why do chromosomes need to condense during prophase rather than remaining as diffuse chromatin?

options.text: Condensed chromosomes can be moved and separated more efficiently by spindle fibres
options.explanation: Condensation makes chromosomes compact and manageable for attachment to and movement by spindle microtubules.

options.text: Condensation allows chromosomes to replicate during the mitotic phase itself
options.explanation: Replication occurs during S phase, not during mitosis. Condensation aids in movement and separation.

options.text: Diffuse chromatin would dissolve in the cytoplasm without a nuclear membrane
options.explanation: Chromatin does not dissolve; condensation aids in mechanical handling during division.

options.text: Condensation is a random process that has no functional significance at all
options.explanation: Condensation is essential for efficient chromosome separation during mitosis.

toLevel3.question: What is the functional significance of centromere splitting during anaphase?

options.text: It releases sister chromatids so each can be pulled to an opposite pole as a separate chromosome
options.explanation: Centromere splitting separates the two sister chromatids, allowing each to move to opposite poles.

options.text: It destroys the chromosome so that new DNA can be synthesised for daughter cells
options.explanation: Centromere splitting separates chromatids; it does not destroy chromosomes or trigger new synthesis.

options.text: It triggers DNA replication to produce additional copies of each chromosome
options.explanation: DNA replication occurs during S phase; centromere splitting separates already-replicated chromatids.

options.text: It fuses the two chromatids together into one thicker chromosome permanently
options.explanation: Centromere splitting separates chromatids; it does not fuse them together.

toLevel3.question: Why is the reformation of nuclear membranes during telophase necessary for cell function?

options.text: It re-establishes separate nuclear compartments that protect and regulate each set of DNA
options.explanation: Nuclear membranes create distinct compartments that protect DNA and regulate gene expression in each daughter cell.

options.text: It provides structural support for the cell membrane during cytokinesis only
options.explanation: Nuclear membrane reformation protects DNA, not the cell membrane.

options.text: It prevents chromosomes from condensing again in the following cell cycle
options.explanation: Nuclear membranes do not prevent condensation; chromosomes will condense again if the cell divides.

options.text: It has no functional significance and is simply a leftover from earlier stages
options.explanation: Nuclear membrane reformation is essential for creating functional nuclei in daughter cells.

toLevel3.question: Chromosomes condense during prophase so they can be efficiently attached to and moved by spindle fibres during later mitotic stages.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Condensation makes chromosomes compact enough for spindle attachment and orderly separation.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. Condensation is functionally important for mechanical handling during mitosis.

toLevel3.question: In interphase, the nucleus appears {{blank:1}} with a dark mass inside, whereas in prophase, individual {{blank:2}} become visible.

options.text: intact
options.explanation: In interphase, the nuclear membrane is intact and the nucleus appears as a distinct structure.

options.text: absent
options.explanation: The nucleus is present and intact during interphase; it breaks down during prophase.

options.text: divided
options.explanation: The nucleus is intact as a single structure during interphase.

options.text: chromosomes
options.explanation: As chromatin condenses during prophase, individual chromosomes become visible.

options.text: ribosomes
options.explanation: Ribosomes are not the structures that become visible; condensed chromosomes are.

options.text: membranes
options.explanation: The nuclear membrane breaks down during prophase; it is the chromosomes that become visible.

toLevel3.question: Chromosomes condense so they can be {{blank:1}} efficiently by spindle fibres during {{blank:2}} and anaphase.

options.text: moved
options.explanation: Condensed chromosomes are compact enough to be moved by spindle microtubules during division.

options.text: dissolved
options.explanation: Chromosomes are moved, not dissolved, during mitosis.

options.text: replicated
options.explanation: Replication occurs in S phase; condensation aids movement during mitosis.

options.text: metaphase
options.explanation: During metaphase, chromosomes are moved to align at the equator by spindle fibres.

options.text: S phase
options.explanation: S phase is for DNA replication; chromosome movement by spindles occurs during metaphase and anaphase.

options.text: G1 phase
options.explanation: G1 is a growth phase; chromosome movement by spindle fibres occurs during mitosis.

toLevel3.question: Centromere splitting during anaphase releases {{blank:1}} chromatids so each can become a separate {{blank:2}}.

options.text: sister
options.explanation: Sister chromatids are the two identical copies joined at the centromere; splitting releases them.

options.text: parent
options.explanation: The term is sister chromatids, not parent chromatids.

options.text: random
options.explanation: The chromatids are specifically sister chromatids, identical copies joined at the centromere.

options.text: chromosome
options.explanation: Once separated, each sister chromatid is now considered an individual chromosome.

options.text: organelle
options.explanation: Separated chromatids become individual chromosomes, not organelles.

options.text: nucleus
options.explanation: Each separated chromatid becomes a chromosome; nuclei re-form later during telophase.

toLevel4.question: A student views a cell under a microscope and sees chromosomes lined up in a single row across the middle of the cell. Which stage of mitosis is this cell in?

options.text: Metaphase, because chromosomes are aligned at the metaphase plate
options.explanation: Chromosomes aligned at the cell equator is the defining feature of metaphase.

options.text: Prophase, because chromosomes are first becoming visible at this stage
options.explanation: In prophase, chromosomes condense but are scattered, not aligned at the equator.

options.text: Anaphase, because chromosomes are moving towards the centre of the cell
options.explanation: In anaphase, chromatids move to the poles, not align at the centre.

options.text: Telophase, because chromosomes are gathering before nuclear membrane forms
options.explanation: In telophase, chromosomes are at the poles decondensing, not aligned at the centre.

toLevel4.question: A micrograph shows a cell with V-shaped structures being pulled towards opposite ends of the cell. Which stage of mitosis is this?

options.text: Anaphase, because sister chromatids are being pulled to opposite poles
options.explanation: V-shaped chromosomes moving to opposite poles is characteristic of anaphase, as spindle fibres pull chromatids.

options.text: Metaphase, because chromosomes are moving to align at the cell equator
options.explanation: In metaphase, chromosomes are aligned at the equator, not moving to opposite ends.

options.text: Prophase, because chromatin is condensing into visible chromosome shapes
options.explanation: In prophase, chromosomes condense but are not yet being pulled to opposite poles.

options.text: Telophase, because chromosomes are decondensing at the cell poles now
options.explanation: In telophase, chromosomes are decondensing at the poles; V-shaped movement indicates anaphase.

toLevel4.question: A cell treated with a drug that prevents spindle fibre formation is observed. The chromosomes are condensed but scattered throughout the cell. What stage is this cell arrested in?

options.text: Prometaphase/late prophase, because without spindles chromosomes cannot align at the equator
options.explanation: Without spindle fibres, chromosomes condense but cannot be moved to the metaphase plate for alignment.

options.text: Telophase, because the cell has completed chromosome separation already
options.explanation: Without spindles, chromosomes cannot separate; the cell is stuck before alignment.

options.text: Anaphase, because chromatids are scattered as they move to opposite poles
options.explanation: Chromatid movement requires spindle fibres; without them, the cell cannot reach anaphase.

options.text: Interphase, because the cell has not yet begun any stage of mitosis
options.explanation: The chromosomes are condensed, indicating the cell has entered mitosis but cannot progress without spindles.

toLevel4.question: A student counts cells in a tissue sample and finds most cells have an intact nucleus with no visible individual chromosomes. What phase are most of these cells in?

options.text: Interphase, because the nucleus is intact and chromatin is not condensed
options.explanation: An intact nucleus with no visible individual chromosomes indicates interphase, where DNA exists as diffuse chromatin.

options.text: Prophase, because the nucleus is still present during early prophase
options.explanation: In prophase, individual chromosomes become visible and the nuclear membrane begins to break down.

options.text: Telophase, because nuclear membranes have just reformed around chromatin
options.explanation: While nuclei reform in telophase, most cells in a sample are in interphase since it is the longest phase.

options.text: Metaphase, because chromosomes are hidden behind the metaphase plate
options.explanation: In metaphase, chromosomes are visible and aligned; they are not hidden.

toLevel4.question: A diagram shows a cell with two groups of chromosomes at opposite ends and nuclear membranes beginning to form around each group. Which stage is this?

options.text: Telophase, because nuclear membranes are reforming around separated chromosome groups
options.explanation: Two groups of chromosomes at the poles with reforming nuclear membranes is the defining feature of telophase.

options.text: Anaphase, because chromosomes are still moving to opposite poles of the cell
options.explanation: In anaphase, chromosomes are actively moving; nuclear membrane reformation indicates telophase.

options.text: Prophase, because the nuclear membrane is breaking down around the chromosomes
options.explanation: In prophase, the membrane breaks down. Reformation of membranes occurs during telophase.

options.text: Metaphase, because chromosomes are positioned at two ends of the metaphase plate
options.explanation: In metaphase, chromosomes are aligned at the centre, not at opposite ends.

toLevel4.question: A researcher uses a time-lapse video to observe cell division. They note the moment when condensed chromosomes first appear and the nucleus is no longer visible. Which transition are they observing?

options.text: The transition from interphase to prophase
options.explanation: The appearance of condensed chromosomes and disappearance of the nuclear membrane marks entry into prophase.

options.text: The transition from metaphase to anaphase
options.explanation: The metaphase-to-anaphase transition involves chromosome separation, not initial condensation.

options.text: The transition from anaphase to telophase
options.explanation: The anaphase-to-telophase transition involves chromosomes arriving at poles and decondensing.

options.text: The transition from telophase to cytokinesis
options.explanation: The telophase-to-cytokinesis transition involves cytoplasm division, not chromosome condensation.

toLevel4.question: An error occurs during anaphase where one chromatid fails to separate from its sister. What would be the result in the daughter cells?

options.text: One daughter cell would have an extra chromosome and the other would be missing one
options.explanation: Non-disjunction during anaphase results in unequal chromosome distribution between daughter cells.

options.text: Both daughter cells would have the normal number of chromosomes regardless
options.explanation: Failure to separate means one cell gets both copies and the other gets none of that chromosome.

options.text: Both daughter cells would receive double the normal chromosome number
options.explanation: Only one daughter cell would receive the extra chromosome; the other would be deficient.

options.text: The cell would immediately return to metaphase and attempt separation again
options.explanation: Once anaphase has begun, the cell does not reverse to metaphase.

toLevel4.question: A cell showing chromosomes aligned in a single row at the equator is in {{blank:1}}, while V-shaped chromosomes moving to opposite ends indicates {{blank:2}}.

options.text: metaphase
options.explanation: Chromosome alignment at the equator is the defining visual feature of metaphase.

options.text: prophase
options.explanation: In prophase, chromosomes are condensing but not yet aligned at the equator.

options.text: telophase
options.explanation: In telophase, chromosomes are at the poles decondensing, not aligned at the equator.

options.text: anaphase
options.explanation: V-shaped chromosomes being pulled to opposite poles is the characteristic appearance of anaphase.

options.text: metaphase
options.explanation: In metaphase, chromosomes are stationary at the equator, not moving to poles.

options.text: prophase
options.explanation: In prophase, chromosomes are condensing, not being pulled to opposite poles.

toLevel4.question: An intact nucleus with no visible individual chromosomes indicates {{blank:1}}, while condensed chromosomes without a nuclear membrane indicates {{blank:2}}.

options.text: interphase
options.explanation: In interphase, the nucleus is intact and DNA exists as diffuse chromatin, not visible chromosomes.

options.text: telophase
options.explanation: While nuclei reform in telophase, condensed chromosomes are still visible initially.

options.text: anaphase
options.explanation: In anaphase, chromosomes are visible and being separated; there is no intact nucleus.

options.text: prophase
options.explanation: Condensed chromosomes with no nuclear membrane is the key visual indicator of prophase.

options.text: interphase
options.explanation: In interphase, the nuclear membrane is intact and individual chromosomes are not visible.

options.text: metaphase
options.explanation: While metaphase also lacks a nuclear membrane, the chromosomes are specifically aligned at the equator.

toLevel4.question: If a chromatid fails to separate during anaphase, one daughter cell receives an {{blank:1}} chromosome while the other is {{blank:2}} one.

options.text: extra
options.explanation: The cell that receives both chromatids ends up with an extra copy of that chromosome.

options.text: identical
options.explanation: While the chromatids are identical, the issue is that one cell gets an extra copy.

options.text: damaged
options.explanation: The chromosome is not necessarily damaged; the problem is unequal distribution.

options.text: missing
options.explanation: The other daughter cell does not receive a copy of that chromosome, so it is missing one.

options.text: gaining
options.explanation: The other cell loses a chromosome; it does not gain one.

options.text: doubling
options.explanation: The other cell is deficient, not doubling. Only one cell gets the extra chromosome.

toLevel5.question: A student examines a tissue sample and needs to determine the mitotic index. They identify cells in each stage. Why would most cells in a rapidly dividing tissue appear to be in interphase rather than mitosis?

options.text: Interphase is the longest part of the cell cycle, so cells spend more time there even when dividing rapidly
options.explanation: Even in rapidly dividing tissues, interphase (G1, S, G2) takes far longer than mitosis, so more cells are captured in interphase.

options.text: Most cells in rapidly dividing tissue have stopped dividing and entered G0 permanently
options.explanation: In rapidly dividing tissue, cells are actively cycling, not entering G0. Interphase is simply longer.

options.text: Interphase cells are easier to identify, so the student is miscounting the mitotic cells
options.explanation: The observation is correct; interphase is genuinely longer, making more cells appear in that phase.

options.text: Rapidly dividing cells skip interphase entirely and spend all their time in mitosis
options.explanation: Cells cannot skip interphase; DNA replication during S phase is required before each division.

toLevel5.question: Compare the events of prophase and telophase. What pattern emerges from this comparison?

options.text: Telophase reverses the events of prophase: chromosomes decondense and nuclear membranes reform
options.explanation: Prophase and telophase are mirror processes: prophase disassembles the nucleus, and telophase reassembles it.

options.text: Prophase and telophase involve identical events occurring at the same time in division
options.explanation: They involve opposite events: condensation versus decondensation, breakdown versus reformation.

options.text: Telophase has no relationship to prophase and involves completely unrelated processes
options.explanation: Telophase directly reverses prophase events, showing a clear functional relationship.

options.text: Prophase reverses the events of telophase from the previous cell cycle division
options.explanation: While prophase undoes the state established by the previous telophase, the direct comparison shows telophase as the reverse of prophase.

toLevel5.question: A researcher observes that a cancer cell line has a higher proportion of cells in metaphase compared to normal tissue. What might explain this observation?

options.text: The cancer cells may have a partially functional M checkpoint that delays progression from metaphase to anaphase
options.explanation: A slow M checkpoint or attachment difficulties could cause cancer cells to spend longer in metaphase, increasing the observed proportion.

options.text: Cancer cells spend more time in metaphase because they have fewer chromosomes to align
options.explanation: Cancer cells often have more chromosomes (aneuploidy), not fewer, which could delay alignment.

options.text: Normal cells do not go through metaphase so only cancer cells show this stage
options.explanation: All dividing cells pass through metaphase; cancer cells may simply spend more time in this stage.

options.text: Cancer cells skip metaphase entirely, so the observation must be a counting error
options.explanation: Cancer cells do go through metaphase; the observation of more cells in metaphase is biologically plausible.

toLevel5.question: Colchicine is a drug that prevents spindle fibre formation. If applied to dividing cells, at which stage would you expect cells to accumulate, and why?

options.text: Metaphase, because chromosomes condense but cannot be aligned or separated without spindle fibres
options.explanation: Without spindles, chromosomes condense during prophase but cannot progress past metaphase, causing accumulation.

options.text: Telophase, because spindle fibres are needed for nuclear membrane reformation at the poles
options.explanation: Nuclear membrane reformation does not require spindle fibres; spindles are needed for chromosome movement.

options.text: G1 phase, because spindle fibres are needed before DNA replication can begin in the cell
options.explanation: Spindle fibres function during mitosis, not G1. Colchicine affects cells during division.

options.text: S phase, because DNA polymerase requires spindle proteins to function during replication
options.explanation: DNA polymerase does not require spindle proteins. Colchicine affects mitotic spindle formation.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why anaphase is typically the shortest stage of mitosis. How does this relate to the mechanism of chromosome separation?

options.text: Rapid chromatid separation is driven by spindle fibre shortening, which is a fast mechanical process
options.explanation: Spindle fibres shorten by depolymerisation, quickly pulling chromatids apart once centromeres split.

options.text: Anaphase is short because no important events occur and chromosomes simply drift apart
options.explanation: Anaphase involves active, rapid chromosome separation by spindle fibres, not passive drifting.

options.text: Anaphase is actually the longest stage of mitosis, not the shortest in duration
options.explanation: Anaphase is typically the shortest stage; the rapid mechanical separation is completed quickly.

options.text: Anaphase duration depends on cell size and has no relation to the separation mechanism
options.explanation: While cell size can influence timing, the rapid shortening of spindle fibres makes anaphase inherently brief.

toLevel5.question: A student argues that the PMAT mnemonic is misleading because it implies four distinct, separate events, when in reality the stages form a continuous process. Evaluate this argument.

options.text: The argument is valid; mitosis is continuous but PMAT helps identify key events within that continuum
options.explanation: Mitosis is a smooth, continuous process. PMAT identifies recognisable stages within it for study and identification.

options.text: The argument is invalid; the four stages are completely separate events with clear pauses
options.explanation: Mitosis flows continuously from one stage to the next without distinct pauses between stages.

options.text: The argument is invalid because PMAT includes stages that do not actually occur at all
options.explanation: All four PMAT stages occur; the student's point is about the continuous nature of the process.

options.text: The argument is valid and PMAT should be replaced with a single-stage description entirely
options.explanation: While mitosis is continuous, PMAT is useful for identifying key landmark events; removing it would reduce clarity.

toLevel5.question: How would you use the relative proportions of cells in each mitotic stage to estimate the duration of each stage?

options.text: Stages with more cells take longer, because cells spend more time in longer stages and are more likely to be observed there
options.explanation: The proportion of cells in a stage reflects its duration relative to the total cycle time.

options.text: Stages with fewer cells take longer, because cells move through long stages too fast to be observed
options.explanation: Cells in longer stages are observed more often because they remain in that stage for more time.

options.text: Cell proportions cannot be used to estimate stage duration under any circumstances
options.explanation: This is a standard technique; proportions directly reflect relative time spent in each stage.

options.text: All stages have equal proportions because they all take the same amount of time
options.explanation: Stages vary in duration; interphase is longest and anaphase is typically shortest.

toLevel5.question: Compare the consequences of an error during metaphase alignment versus an error during anaphase separation. Which has a greater impact on daughter cell viability?

options.text: Both can cause non-viable daughter cells, but anaphase errors are more direct because separation has already begun
options.explanation: Metaphase alignment errors may be caught by the M checkpoint, but once anaphase begins, errors in separation directly produce aneuploid cells.

options.text: Metaphase errors are always caught by checkpoints, so only anaphase errors cause any problems
options.explanation: While the M checkpoint catches many metaphase errors, it is not infallible; some alignment errors can persist.

options.text: Anaphase errors have no impact because cells can correct chromosome distribution after division
options.explanation: Daughter cells cannot correct chromosome number after division; anaphase errors produce permanent aneuploidy.

options.text: Neither type of error affects daughter cell viability because mitosis is a self-correcting process
options.explanation: Mitosis has checkpoints but is not fully self-correcting; errors in either stage can produce non-viable cells.

toLevel5.question: Colchicine causes cells to accumulate in {{blank:1}} because without spindle fibres, chromosomes cannot be {{blank:2}} or separated.

options.text: metaphase
options.explanation: Without spindle fibres, chromosomes cannot align at the equator or be pulled apart, arresting cells at metaphase.

options.text: telophase
options.explanation: Cells cannot reach telophase without completing anaphase, which requires spindle fibres.

options.text: interphase
options.explanation: Colchicine affects spindle formation during mitosis, not interphase processes.

options.text: aligned
options.explanation: Spindle fibres are needed to move chromosomes to the metaphase plate for alignment.

options.text: replicated
options.explanation: Replication occurs during S phase and does not require spindle fibres.

options.text: condensed
options.explanation: Condensation occurs independently of spindle fibres during prophase.

toLevel5.question: The proportion of cells in each mitotic stage can estimate stage {{blank:1}} because cells are more likely to be observed in {{blank:2}} stages.

options.text: duration
options.explanation: Higher proportions indicate longer duration because cells spend more time in those stages.

options.text: location
options.explanation: Proportions indicate time spent, not physical location of the stages.

options.text: energy
options.explanation: Proportions reflect time, not energy expenditure during each stage.

options.text: longer
options.explanation: Cells spend more time in longer stages, so more cells are captured in those stages at any snapshot.

options.text: shorter
options.explanation: Fewer cells are observed in shorter stages because cells pass through them quickly.

options.text: earlier
options.explanation: The proportion reflects duration, not position in the sequence.
